description: Your child was hurt at a relative’s house over the holidays. How a Georgia homeowner’s insurance claim works, and how to protect the family.
shortAnswer: You are claiming against the insurance, not against Grandma. Most homeowner’s policies cover a guest who is hurt on the property, and in most of these cases your relative does not pay a dime. A Christmas visit almost never makes a grandparent a parent for immunity purposes.

sections.heading: The short answer: you are claiming against the insurance, not against Grandma
sections.shortAnswer: The insurance company investigates the claim, defends your relative, and pays any settlement up to the policy limits. If a lawsuit has to be filed, it is filed in your relative’s name, but most of these claims settle without one.

sections.heading: There may also be a small no-fault benefit
sections.shortAnswer: Many homeowner’s policies include medical payments to others coverage, which pays a guest’s reasonable medical bills regardless of fault, usually up to a few thousand dollars.

sections.heading: What Georgia law says the homeowner owed your child
sections.shortAnswer: A social guest is a licensee under O.C.G.A. § 51-3-2, which narrows the owner’s duty. But a relative who took charge of your child, the attractive nuisance rule, and the dog bite statute often matter more than that label.

sections.heading: What about grandparents? Isn’t there a family immunity?
sections.shortAnswer: Georgia courts have said grandparents, simply as grandparents, do not stand in the place of parents. Immunity has applied only when a grandparent was really raising the child.

sections.heading: When the child who caused it was a cousin
sections.shortAnswer: Georgia makes parents liable for a child’s willful or malicious acts up to a statutory limit, and parents can be liable for their own negligence. The cousin’s parents’ policy and the host’s policy may both apply.

sections.heading: The traps
sections.shortAnswer: Household exclusions, late notice, the cooperation clause, the “Where were you?” question, and recorded statements all trip families up.

sections.heading: Keeping the family together
sections.shortAnswer: Explain early that the claim is against the policy, report it right away, keep fault off the family group text, and settle within the policy limits so your relative’s savings are never at risk.

sections.heading: What I tell parents
sections.shortAnswer: Get your child treated, photograph the hazard, get the insurance information from your relative, do not give a recorded statement before you get advice, and watch your own deadline.

faq.q: Can I make a claim against a grandparent’s homeowner’s insurance in Georgia if my child was hurt at their house?
faq.a: Yes. Most homeowner’s policies include liability coverage for guests who are hurt on the property. The insurance company investigates, defends your relative, and pays any settlement up to the policy limits. In most of these cases, your relative does not pay a dime.

faq.q: Does parental immunity protect a grandparent from my child’s injury claim in Georgia?
faq.a: Usually not. Georgia courts have said grandparents, simply as grandparents, do not stand in the place of parents. Immunity has applied when a grandparent was actually raising the child, such as a legal guardian, but a holiday visit almost never makes a grandparent a parent.

faq.q: What duty does a Georgia homeowner owe a child who is a social guest?
faq.a: A social guest is a licensee under O.C.G.A. § 51-3-2, which narrows the owner’s duty. But if the relative agreed to watch the child, the relative had a duty to use reasonable care in supervising the child, and the attractive nuisance rule and the dog bite statute may also apply.
